text: Every morning at Analog Devices Thailand, one question must be answered before work can go on.
Which tester should get its next lot of wafers?
Answering it used to take more than 90 minutes.
This project brought the round we timed down to 20.
Wafer Sort tests every die on a wafer, before assembly.
Wafers travel in sets called lots.
Every lot is moved, prepared and checked by a Material Handler, or MH.
At the CSP station, three MH on each shift look after 84 testers.
First, MH decide which lots to withdraw from the Die Bank.
Then they push a cart from the MH station to the pass box, and collect six to eight lots: FOUPs and canisters.
At the desk they check each lot, print the setup sheet and make the ink map: about 14 minutes.
The Ricmar moves the wafers from a canister into a black FOUP: about 6 minutes of MH work.
An operator takes the lot to the tester. Testing takes minutes or days, with no MH work.
After each test step, MH check the map: usually twice, 14 minutes each.
Then QA, and back to the Die Bank. About an hour of MH work for every lot.
Where does a shift go? We logged the three MH on the floor.
Check Map alone is about half of their work, but fixing it means changing several systems.
The withdrawal decision is only 7 percent. But it is reading and adding by hand, and it decides whether a tester gets its next lot on time.
So we fixed that first.
This is how the decision is made today, one tester at a time.
Open the EWB board and find the tester.
Read its lot: 25 wafers left, and 43 hours of work.
Then open Statusphere, the tester's own log: is the real time close to the plan?
Then judge, by a rule kept in memory. MH call it “plus six”: bring the next lot if the tester runs out before 1 a.m., 18 hours from the start of the shift.
This tester has more than 18 hours of work left, so its next lot waits.
Now do that for more than 80 testers: more than 90 minutes, every round.
Why does it matter? A tester can only run if a lot is waiting.
MH are already busy about 97 percent of the shift.
And a rule in memory cannot be checked. Scored against the lots MH really took, “plus six” listed only 61 percent.
Our idea: let a script do the reading and the adding, with one written rule.
Add the hours left on the running lot, plus the lots already waiting at the tester.
If the total is under a threshold, withdraw the next lot.
MH get one list, and still decide.
Which threshold? Every morning we saved the EWB, and the lots MH really took.
We tried five windows and picked 24 hours.
Then we tested it blind: the list was saved each morning and never shown to MH. It caught 82 percent of the lots MH took, against 54 for the old rule.
Later we ran the backtest once more, on all the data up to that day. It gave 24 and a half hours.
Tested blind again on seven new days, it held: 85 percent.
This is the real thing. We take the hours on the EWB, apply our rule, and get the list: every lot to withdraw, most urgent first.
MH tick each lot they withdraw.
If they don't, they write why. And if they take a lot that is not on the list, they write why too.
This green and red board is a prototype: the same list, inside the EWB that MH already know.
The results. The decision round went from more than 90 minutes to 20, the best case in the day round we timed.
On seven new days, 85 percent of the lots MH took were on the list, against 56 for the old rule.
The target is 90, so we keep tracking.
That gives back about 140 minutes a day.
By our model, the same team could serve about 13 more testers: cost avoided, not a job cut.
And the rule is now written down. Anyone gets the same list, and MH still decide.
